newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Signs mount of an early arrival of next El Nino.
newsitem.headline: Signs mount of an early arrival of next El Nino.

text.p: Evidence is mounting that an El Nino phenomenon is affecting global weather, which for Australia means drought across most of its agricultural belts, a U.S. scientist said on Tuesday.
"It will have a dramatic impact on Australia's agricultural sector," John Kermond of the Washington-based National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration told Reuters in Melbourne.
As a result, forecasts for Australian agricultural production are expected to be revised downward to take the latest El Nino into account
Record wheat production in Australia last year was unlikely to be repeated under emerging El Nino conditions and sugar, cotton and livestock were also likely to suffer, he said.
The Austalian Wheat Board has already forecast revised down its latest estimate to 16.3 million tonnes from 19.3 million.

Kermond, who is attending an international conference in Melbourne said too little is known about the latest El Nino to predict the duration of the pattern other than it appears to have been set in motion much earlier than usual.
"We're seeing all of the standard El Nino patterns now that would normally would have started to come out in December," Kermond said.
Researchers liken the change in timing to "Mother Nature readjusting her thermostat," he said.
Abnormally dry weather in Alaska, changing migration patterns among sea birds and measurably higher ocean water temperatures all suggest the onslaught of El Nino, he said.

"The strongest El Nino in recent times occurred in 1982-83 costing some US$13 billion in damage around the world and we think this event could be as strong or certainly close to as strong as that even," Kermond said.
The term El Nino, Spanish for "Christ Child" was originally used by fishermen in Ecuador and Peru to refer to warm ocean current that typically appears around Christmas.

It also threatens dry weather in Southeast Asia, particularly Indonesia, and Papua New Guinea. And typically, when it produces bushfires and drought in eastern Australia, El Nino also brings rains and floods in California.
"You don't have to be a rocket scientist to know that when you've got warmer ocean temperatures in numerous spots that an El Nino coming," Kermond said.

A string of 69 permanent buoys anchored across the equatorial Pacific region have been detecting warmer water and satellites have recorded a higher-than normal sea waves marching across the far western Pacific Ocean toward North and South America.
"That's massive amounts of water migrating across the equatorial Pacific and that's another reson why we think this El Nino will be strong," Kermond said.
